title: Site brief and access sheet for each client (editable template)
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Owners, supervisors and office staff who collect site information before a first visit, and who set the rules the team follows inside a client's home or workplace
learningOutcomes: Record access, keys, alarms and pets so the team can enter and leave a site without relying on memory
Identify site hazards and name the control the business will use for each one before the first visit
Store access details in a way that protects the client's privacy and security

instruction.heading: What the brief is for
instruction.body: The site brief is one record that the office and the team read before anyone arrives. It replaces the conversation at the door and the note left on the bench. Its job is to answer the questions that otherwise cause wasted visits: how the team gets in, what is in and out of scope, which items are off limits, what near the work could cause harm, and who to call. A brief is only as good as the walk-through or call that produced it, so every entry records who gave the information and when. The client service agreement (“Client service agreement”) refers to this brief and does not repeat its detail.

instruction.heading: Access and keys without recording secrets
instruction.body: Record how the team gets in: a key held by the office, a lock box, a code, or the client present. Record where the access detail is kept, not the detail itself. A full alarm code or key number written into an open file creates a security exposure for the household and for the firm. The brief can say that the alarm arrangement is held in the business's secure record, and the code is kept in the approved store. Record who may give instructions on the day, and what the team does if access fails: which number to call, and that the team does not wait outside for an unknown period.

instruction.heading: Preparation, requests and items the team will not handle
instruction.body: Clients are often asked to clear items that delay the work: papers on desks, items on floors, valuables, and rooms they do not want cleaned. Write each request as a checkable action, such as 'benches clear of papers before arrival', and record what happens when a request is not met. If the team would have to move items, the brief says whether that is included, and any extra time is agreed in writing before the visit. Items the team will not move, such as heavy furniture above the business's own weight limit, appliances that must be pulled out from a wall, or electronics the business does not handle, are written down, as are items that must be left alone. Products the client asks the team to use or avoid are recorded, and any product the client supplies is recorded with the client's responsibility for it.

instruction.heading: Pets, occupants and the team's rule
instruction.body: Each animal in the home is listed with its usual location and whether it is secured during the visit. Ask about every animal at each visit, including animals the client says are no trouble. Animals can act differently when the household is out, so the brief records what the client expects. If an animal appears to threaten the team, the team does not enter, and the office contacts the client. The business does not provide childcare or pet care, and this is listed as an exclusion. The arrangement for children and visitors is recorded, together with the business's policy on who may be in the home during the work.

instruction.heading: Site hazards and the controls that go with them
instruction.body: A site hazard is anything that could injure a team member or damage the property. Examples include stairs without rails, slippery tiles, unstable shelving, a pool or spa, a roof space, a balcony, animals, sharps, chemicals already on site, electrical equipment and any height the team is not permitted to work at. For each hazard, the brief names the control: the task is not done, the team is told before arrival, a second person is present, or the work is referred to another service. Heights and manual handling limits come from the business's own risk assessment. Work at height and some chemicals may need a licence or authorisation, which this lesson does not grant.

instruction.heading: Keeping the brief current
instruction.body: A brief expires when the site changes. Set a review date and check it before each scheduled visit. Update the brief when the access method, the alarm arrangement, the pets or a hazard changes. Each change records the date, the person who gave the information and the person who approved it, and creates a new version number. The client confirms the brief before the first visit, and the confirmation is kept with the record.

procedure: Enter the client's name and the site address, and record who gave the information, how, and the date.
Describe the access method and where the access detail is kept, without writing the code or key number itself.
Record the alarm arrangement and the number to call if access fails on the day.
List each room or area in scope, marking any area the client asks the team to leave alone.
Write the client's preparation actions as checkable actions, and record the items the team will not move or handle.
List each animal, its location, whether it is secured, and what the client has said about its behaviour.
Record the arrangement for other occupants and children, and the team rule for an animal or person that makes the site unsafe.
Enter each site hazard with its control, its owner and its review date, using the risk assessment.
Record the PPE and products for the site, and the emergency and escalation contacts.
Enter the review date and version, send the brief to the client, and record their confirmation before the first visit.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is due at a home with an alarm, a lock box and a dog that is sometimes shut in the laundry. The client says the dog is fine with people.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the brief record the alarm, the lock box and the dog, and what should the team do if the dog is loose when they arrive?
workedExamples.reasoning: The alarm entry records that the arrangement is held in the secure record and that the client confirms it is off or changed before each visit. The code itself is not written in the brief. The lock box entry records where the box is and who holds its key, not the combination. For the dog, the entry records its usual location, whether it is secured during the visit, and what the client has said about its behaviour. The client's statement is not an observation, so the office confirms the dog's behaviour with the client in writing before the first visit. The team rule says the team does not enter if an animal appears to be a threat, and the office contacts the client.

equipmentAndPpe: Client's written access and alarm details, held in the secure record and not in this brief
Site walk-through checklist, or call notes with the date and the name of the person spoken to
Risk assessment for site hazards and for heights and manual handling
Lock box or key register reference for the property
PPE for the site as set by the business: see the required PPE field in this brief

commonErrors.error: Writing the alarm code or key number into the brief.
commonErrors.prevention: Record where the code or key is held and who holds it. Keep the detail in the approved secure store.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a verbal access instruction.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm access in writing before the first visit and again after any change.

commonErrors.error: Leaving an animal off the brief because the client says it is no trouble.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask about every animal at each visit, list each one, and record the answers.

commonErrors.error: Recording a hazard with no control.
commonErrors.prevention: Every hazard has a control, a named owner and a review date. A hazard with no control stops the visit until one is recorded.

commonErrors.error: Using a brief after the site has changed.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the review date before each visit, and create a new version whenever a detail changes.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Privacy: access details, keys, alarm arrangements and personal information about occupants are handled under privacy obligations. Check whether the Privacy Act 1988 applies to the business, and what storage rules follow, against a current source, and record the date.
Work health and safety: the business must identify and control site hazards, and the controls must come from a documented risk assessment.
Animals: where an animal may threaten the team, the team withdraws and the office acts. The rule and any fee are set by the business and the agreement.

Some site work, such as work at height or the use of regulated chemicals, may need a licence or authorisation. This lesson covers how to record the site information for that work. It does not grant or confirm any licence, and completing it does not authorise any regulated work.

qualityStandard: Every field is completed, or marked not applicable with a reason in the field
No access code, key number or alarm code is written into the brief
Each hazard has a named control, an owner and a review date
Every animal the client mentions is listed, and the team rule is recorded
The review date is set and falls before the next scheduled visit
The client's confirmation is recorded, with its date and method, before the first visit
documentationEvidence: Completed site brief with its version number, review date and the name of the person who gave and checked the information
Record of where the access detail is kept and who holds it
Risk assessment reference for each hazard listed
Client confirmation of the brief, with date and method
summary: A site brief records where access details are kept, never the details themselves.
Every hazard has a control, and a hazard without one stops the visit.
Every animal is listed, and the team rule for animals is written down.
A brief expires when the site changes, so it carries a review date.

editableTemplates.title: Site brief and access sheet
editableTemplates.purpose: A one-document record, completed before the first visit and reviewed when the site changes, covering access without secrets, the rooms in scope, client preparation, items the team will not handle, animals and occupants, hazards and controls, and the contacts for the day.

fields.label: Client and site address
fields.prompt: Write the client's name and the site address the brief covers.
fields.guidance: The address matches the one in the client service agreement (“Client service agreement”) for the same property.

fields.label: Information source
fields.prompt: Write who gave the information, how it was given (site visit, phone or email), and the date.
fields.guidance: Names the person and the date. Client statements are marked as client-stated, and observations as team-observed.

fields.label: Access method
fields.prompt: Describe how the team enters and leaves: key, lock box, code, or client present. Say where the access detail is kept, not what it is.
fields.guidance: Never the code or key number itself. Names who holds the access detail and the secure place it is kept.

fields.label: Alarm arrangement
fields.prompt: State whether the site has an alarm, and what the team must do before entering and before leaving.
fields.guidance: Says who switches the alarm on or off, and where the arrangement is recorded. The code is not written here.

fields.label: Contact if access fails
fields.prompt: Name the person to call if access fails on the day, and the number to use.
fields.guidance: Uses a number the office monitors on the day. The team does not wait outside for an unknown period.

fields.label: Rooms and areas in scope
fields.prompt: One row per room or area. Columns: area, in scope (yes or no), any client request for that area.
fields.guidance: Every area in the scope of the agreement is listed. An area the client asks the team to leave alone is recorded as no.

fields.label: Client preparation
fields.prompt: List what the client agrees to do before the team arrives, such as clearing floors, securing valuables and closing rooms. Write each item as a checkable action.
fields.guidance: Each item is an action with a clear end state, such as benches clear of papers. The team's response if an item is not done is stated.

fields.label: Items the team will not move or handle
fields.prompt: List the items the team will not move, handle or clean, and give the reason in one line.
fields.guidance: Includes heavy furniture above the business weight limit, appliances that are fixed or must be pulled out, electronics the business does not handle, and items of high personal or financial value.

fields.label: Products requested or supplied by the client
fields.prompt: Record any product the client asks the team to use or avoid, and any product the client supplies.
fields.guidance: Client-supplied products are recorded. The client's responsibility for them is the one the agreement sets out.

fields.label: Animals in the home
fields.prompt: One row per animal. Columns: animal, usual location, secured during the visit (yes or no), what the client has said about its behaviour.
fields.guidance: Every animal is listed, including animals the client says are no trouble. The team rule for animals is recorded in f12.

fields.label: Other occupants and children
fields.prompt: State who will be in the home during the visit, the client's arrangement for children and visitors, and the business policy on occupants.
fields.guidance: The business does not provide childcare or pet care. The arrangement is one the team can work with safely.

fields.label: Team rule for animals or occupants
fields.prompt: Write the rule the team follows if an animal or person makes the site unsafe, and what the office does next.
fields.guidance: The team withdraws, the office contacts the client, and any fee is the one the agreement sets out.

fields.label: Site hazards and controls
fields.prompt: One row per hazard. Columns: hazard, who could be affected, control, owner, review date.
fields.guidance: Every hazard has a control that is more than awareness. Height and manual handling limits come from the business risk assessment.

fields.label: PPE and products for this site
fields.prompt: List the PPE the team wears on this site and the products used, referring to the business approved list.
fields.guidance: Matches the business PPE requirement for this kind of job. Products come from the approved list.

fields.label: Emergency and escalation contacts
fields.prompt: Name who is called in an emergency at the site, and who the team escalates to if a problem is not solved on the day.
fields.guidance: Contacts are roles with numbers the office monitors. An emergency is handled by emergency services first, then the office is told.

fields.label: Review date and version
fields.prompt: Enter the review date and the version number of this brief.
fields.guidance: The review date falls before the next scheduled visit. Any change creates a new version.

fields.label: Client confirmation
fields.prompt: Record that the client has confirmed the brief is correct, the date, and the method used.
fields.guidance: Confirmation is recorded before the first visit. A brief the client has not seen is treated as not yet agreed.

levels.meets: The access method names who holds the detail and where it is kept, and contains no code, key number or alarm code.
levels.does_not_meet: A code, key number or alarm code appears in the brief, or the access method is not stated.

levels.meets: Each area is marked in or out, and each preparation request is an action that can be seen as done or not done.
levels.does_not_meet: Requests are general, such as keep things tidy, or an area is not marked.

levels.meets: Each hazard has a control, an owner and a review date.
levels.does_not_meet: A hazard has no control, no owner or no review date.

levels.meets: Every animal the client mentions is listed, and the team rule for animals and occupants is written.
levels.does_not_meet: An animal is left out, or no team rule is written where the client has said there are animals.

levels.meets: The review date, the version and the client confirmation are recorded before the first visit.
levels.does_not_meet: The brief has no review date, or the client has not confirmed it before the first visit.

officialReferences.title: Duties of a PCBU (Safe Work Australia)
officialReferences.covers: Safe Work Australia's PCBU duties page says a PCBU must seek to eliminate risks to health and safety so far as reasonably practicable and, where elimination is not possible, must reduce the risks so far as reasonably practicable, applying the hierarchy of control where required. The page refers only to the model WHS Act and Regulations, not to state and territory WHS wording as adopted.

officialReferences.title: Small business (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: OAIC small business page (published 10 March 2023; last modified 5 September 2024): a small business has an annual turnover of $3 million or less, but regardless of turnover the Privacy Act covers listed businesses, including health service providers and businesses trading in personal information. Whether this business is covered depends on its turnover and activities. The page has no section on storing or securing personal information: storage rules remain UNCONFIRMED.
